title: Electrochemistry: Electrode Potential, Batteries, Fuel Cells and Corrosion
subcategory: Electrochemistry — Electrode Potential, EMF, Nernst Equation, Conductance, Electrolysis, Batteries, Fuel Cells, Corrosion
references: NCERT Chemistry Part I, Class 12 — Electrochemistry
summary: Standard electrode potentials (measured relative to the standard hydrogen electrode) predict a galvanic cell's EMF and reaction feasibility; the Nernst equation extends this to non-standard conditions, and molar conductivity trends distinguish strong from weak electrolytes.
explanation: Standard electrode potential (E°) is measured relative to the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE, arbitrarily assigned E° = 0.00 V), and tabulated as STANDARD REDUCTION potentials by convention — a more positive E° means a stronger tendency to be reduced (a better oxidising agent). For a galvanic cell, standard EMF = E°cathode(reduction) − E°anode(reduction) — using both values as REDUCTION potentials, a very common exam trap being to wrongly reverse the anode's sign twice. A positive cell EMF (equivalently, negative ΔG° = −nFE°cell) confirms the cell reaction is spontaneous as written. The Nernst equation, Ecell = E°cell − (RT/nF) ln Q (or the base-10, 298 K simplified form using 0.0591/n log Q), extends electrode/cell potential to NON-standard concentrations/pressures, explaining why a cell's measured EMF changes as the reaction proceeds and concentrations shift away from standard 1 M/1 atm conditions. At equilibrium, Ecell = 0, and this directly links E°cell to the equilibrium constant K. Molar conductivity (Λm = κ/C, where κ is specific conductance) INCREASES with dilution for both strong and weak electrolytes, but for a very different reason in each: for strong electrolytes, it increases only slightly and levels off at a finite, measurable limiting value (Λm°) because ionic interactions weaken with dilution; for weak electrolytes, it increases sharply and continuously (never quite reaching a directly measurable plateau) because the DEGREE OF DISSOCIATION itself increases with dilution, producing more ions. Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions states that at infinite dilution, each ion contributes a fixed, characteristic value to the total molar conductivity regardless of the other ion present — this lets Λm° for a WEAK electrolyte be calculated indirectly by combining known Λm° values of strong electrolytes, since it can't be measured directly by extrapolation for a weak electrolyte. ELECTROLYTIC CELLS run the opposite of galvanic cells: an EXTERNAL electrical source drives a non-spontaneous redox reaction (electrolysis) — e.g. electrolysis of molten NaCl deposits Na at the cathode (reduction) and liberates Cl₂ at the anode (oxidation). Faraday's laws of electrolysis quantify this: the mass deposited/liberated is directly proportional to the total charge passed (Q = It) and to the substance's equivalent weight, letting the amount of a given electrolysis product be calculated directly from current and time. PRACTICAL BATTERIES fall into two classes: PRIMARY cells (e.g. the dry Leclanché cell, mercury cell) undergo a one-way reaction and CANNOT be recharged, since the reaction products can't be efficiently converted back; SECONDARY cells (e.g. the lead-acid accumulator used in vehicles, the Ni-Cd cell) CAN be recharged by passing current in reverse, driving the discharge reaction backward to regenerate the original electrode materials. A FUEL CELL (e.g. the H₂-O₂ fuel cell used in spacecraft) differs from a normal battery in a key way: reactants (fuel and oxidant) are continuously supplied from an EXTERNAL source rather than being stored internally, so the cell can in principle run indefinitely as long as fuel keeps flowing, and — unlike burning the fuel directly — it converts chemical energy to electrical energy with much higher efficiency, since it avoids the heat-engine (Carnot) efficiency limit of combustion. CORROSION (e.g. iron rusting) is fundamentally an ELECTROCHEMICAL process: at anodic regions on the metal surface, iron is oxidised (Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻); the released electrons travel through the metal to cathodic regions where dissolved atmospheric oxygen is reduced (in the presence of moisture); the Fe²⁺ ions are further oxidised and combine with water to form hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust). Since corrosion requires both moisture AND oxygen, both must be present for iron to rust — this is why iron doesn't rust in completely dry air, or in fully deoxygenated water. Corrosion prevention strategies exploit this electrochemical nature: barrier coatings (paint, grease) exclude moisture/oxygen; GALVANISATION (zinc coating) works by making zinc — a MORE reactive metal — the preferential anode ('sacrificial protection'), so zinc corrodes instead of the iron underneath, even where the coating is scratched.

commonMisconceptions: Reversing sign conventions incorrectly when calculating cell EMF — the standard formula uses BOTH electrode potentials as reduction potentials (cathode minus anode); manually flipping the anode's sign AND then also subtracting is a double-negative error many students make.

Assuming molar conductivity increasing with dilution means the SAME thing for strong and weak electrolytes — for strong electrolytes it's a modest increase toward a directly measurable limit; for weak electrolytes it's a steep, theoretically-unbounded-by-direct-measurement increase due to increasing dissociation.

Believing a negative standard electrode potential means a species cannot be reduced at all — it only means that species is a WEAKER oxidising agent than H⁺/H₂ (the SHE reference); reduction can still occur under sufficiently favourable non-standard conditions or with a strong enough reducing partner.

Assuming a fuel cell is just a small battery — a genuine fuel cell requires CONTINUOUS external fuel/oxidant supply, and does not store fixed reactant amounts internally the way a normal primary or secondary battery does.
examples: In a Daniell cell (Zn/Zn²⁺ ‖ Cu²⁺/Cu), zinc (more negative E°) is oxidised at the anode while copper ions are reduced at the cathode, giving a standard EMF of about 1.10 V.
A dead battery can sometimes work again briefly after resting, because as the reaction proceeds, concentrations of reactants/products shift, changing the EMF per the Nernst equation.

A scratched galvanised (zinc-coated) iron pipe still resists rusting at the scratch, because the exposed zinc — being more reactive than iron — corrodes preferentially as a sacrificial anode, protecting the iron underneath even where the coating is physically broken.
genZNote: Cell EMF = cathode's ego minus anode's ego, both measured as reduction potentials — no exceptions.
